newsitem.title: USA: Buried cannons mark site of ill-fated Texas colony.
newsitem.headline: Buried cannons mark site of ill-fated Texas colony.

text.p: Archaeologists have discovered and excavated eight cannons from the site of Fort Saint Louis, considered the first European settlement in Texas, the state historical commission said on Monday.

The cannons were found buried near a creek along the south Texas coast and marked the site of an ill-fated colony founded by French explorer Robert Cavelier de La Salle as he searched for the mouth of the Mississippi River in 1685.

Historians have long known the approximate location of the fort based on maps made by French and Spanish explorers, but the cannons lay undiscovered until a ranchhand stumbled upon them while scanning the area with a metal detector.

"We'd like to do some systematic excavations. Clear some big areas and excavate pretty extensively to look for features and, to some extent, some artifacts," Curtis Tunnell, executive director of the Texas Historical Commission, told Reuters.

The cannons were discovered last October buried in a pit in thick underbrush along Garcitas Creek near Victoria, Texas about 100 miles (160 km) southwest of Houston. But the find was kept secret while officials secured the site from possible poachers.
The cannons were brought from France aboard La Salle's ship L'Aimable, which was lost at sea during an expedition seeking to establish a French colony at the mouth of the Mississippi.

Instead of reaching Louisiana, La Salle's crew made landfall in south Texas, where most on the expedition died of disease or were killed by Indians. La Salle later was murdered by his men after they set out on foot to find the Mississippi.

As the iron cannons were unearthed last October, archaeologists about 15 miles away were removing the first artifacts from La Belle, one of La Salle's ships discovered sunk in the mud of Matagorda Bay.

Working inside an oval dam built to hold back the bay's waters, crews excavating remains of the ship's hull have recovered an ornate bronze cannon, a skeleton, more than 80 wooded barrels and boxes holding trinkets and pewter dishes.
